claim: Local accumulation of oskar (osk) mRNA in the Drosophila oocyte determines the posterior pole of the future embryo.
source: Local accumulation of oskar (osk) mRNA in the Drosophila oocyte determines the posterior pole of the future embryo.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Microtubules and actin filaments are essential for osk mRNA posterior localization.
source: Two major cytoskeletal components, microtubules and actin filaments, together with a microtubule motor, kinesin-1, and an actin motor, myosin-V, are essential for osk mRNA posterior localization.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is presented as background information.

claim: Kinesin-1 is essential for osk mRNA posterior localization.
source: Two major cytoskeletal components, microtubules and actin filaments, together with a microtubule motor, kinesin-1, and an actin motor, myosin-V, are essential for osk mRNA posterior localization.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is presented as background information.

claim: Myosin-V is essential for osk mRNA posterior localization.
source: Two major cytoskeletal components, microtubules and actin filaments, together with a microtubule motor, kinesin-1, and an actin motor, myosin-V, are essential for osk mRNA posterior localization.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is presented as background information.

claim: Staufen is an RNA-binding protein that colocalizes with osk mRNA.
source: In this study, we use Staufen, an RNA-binding protein that colocalizes with osk mRNA, as a proxy for osk mRNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and is presented as a methodological approach.

claim: Posterior localization of osk/Staufen is determined by competition between kinesin-1 and myosin-V.
source: We demonstrate that posterior localization of osk/Staufen is determined by competition between kinesin-1 and myosin-V.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Kinesin-1 removes osk/Staufen from the cortex along microtubules.
source: While kinesin-1 removes osk/Staufen from the cortex along microtubules, myosin-V anchors osk/Staufen at the cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including optogenetic manipulation and genetic perturbations.

claim: Myosin-V anchors osk/Staufen at the cortex.
source: While kinesin-1 removes osk/Staufen from the cortex along microtubules, myosin-V anchors osk/Staufen at the cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including constitutively active myosin-V experiments.

claim: Myosin-V wins over kinesin-1 at the posterior pole due to low microtubule density at this site.
source: Myosin-V wins over kinesin-1 at the posterior pole due to low microtubule density at this site, while kinesin-1 wins at anterior and lateral positions because they have high density of cortically-anchored microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by optogenetic manipulation of microtubule density and genetic perturbations.

claim: Kinesin-1 wins at anterior and lateral positions because they have high density of cortically-anchored microtubules.
source: Myosin-V wins over kinesin-1 at the posterior pole due to low microtubule density at this site, while kinesin-1 wins at anterior and lateral positions because they have high density of cortically-anchored microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by optogenetic manipulation of microtubule density and genetic perturbations.

claim: Posterior determinants are removed from the anterior and lateral cortex but retained at the posterior pole.
source: As a result, posterior determinants are removed from the anterior and lateral cortex but retained at the posterior pole.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the outcome of kinesin-myosin competition.

claim: Posterior determination of Drosophila oocytes is defined by kinesin-myosin competition, whose outcome is primarily determined by cortical microtubule density.
source: Thus, posterior determination of Drosophila oocytes is defined by kinesin-myosin competition, whose outcome is primarily determined by cortical microtubule density.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Kinesin-1 is a major microtubule motor that transports many types of cargoes, including mRNA-containing granules towards plus-ends of microtubules.
source: Kinesin-1, also known as conventional kinesin, is a major microtubule motor that transports many types of cargoes, including mRNA-containing granules towards plus-ends of microtubules (Verhey and Hammond, 2009; Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-1 is required for the posterior accumulation of osk mRNA in Drosophila oocytes that is essential for embryo posterior determination.
source: Kinesin-1 is required for the posterior accumulation of osk mRNA in Drosophila oocytes that is essential for embryo posterior determination (Brendza et al., 2000; Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Krauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Defects in osk mRNA localization prevent germ cell formation and abdomen specification.
source: Defects in osk mRNA localization prevent germ cell formation and abdomen specification (Lehmann and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Posterior localization of osk mRNA is initially established during mid-oogenesis (late stage 8 to stage 9) and maintained throughout late oogenesis (stage 10B to stage 14).
source: Posterior localization of osk mRNA is initially established during mid-oogenesis (late stage 8 to stage 9) and maintained throughout late oogenesis (stage 10B to stage 14).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Staufen forms ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) with osk mRNA.
source: Staufen, an RNA-binding protein that forms ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) with osk mRNA, is commonly used as a proxy for oskar RNA (referred as 'osk/Staufen' hereafter) (Brendza et al., 2000; Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Erdélyi et al., 1995; Shulman et al., 2000; Lu et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2018; St Johnston et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During mid-oogenesis (stage 7–9), the oocyte forms an anterior-to-posterior gradient of cortical microtubules.
source: During mid-oogenesis (stage 7–9), the oocyte forms an anterior-to-posterior gradient of cortical microtubules (Theurkauf et al., 1992; Clark et al., 1994; Clark et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical microtubules are anchored at the cortex by their minus ends via the minus-end binding protein Patronin and a microtubule-actin crosslinker, Short stop (Shot).
source: These microtubules are anchored at the cortex by their minus ends via the minus-end binding protein Patronin and a microtubule-actin crosslinker, Short stop (Shot) (Nashchekin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Shot is excluded from the posterior cortex in a Par-1-dependent manner.
source: Because Shot is excluded from the posterior cortex in a Par-1-dependent manner, more microtubule minus ends are anchored at the anterior and lateral cortex than at the posterior cortex (Shulman et al., 2000; Nashchekin et al., 2016; Zimyanin et al., 2008; Parton et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: More microtubule minus ends are anchored at the anterior and lateral cortex than at the posterior cortex.
source: Because Shot is excluded from the posterior cortex in a Par-1-dependent manner, more microtubule minus ends are anchored at the anterior and lateral cortex than at the posterior cortex (Shulman et al., 2000; Nashchekin et al., 2016; Zimyanin et al., 2008; Parton et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The anterior-posterior cortical microtubule gradient is established in stage 7–8 oocytes.
source: This anterior-posterior cortical microtubule gradient is established in stage 7–8 oocytes (Theurkauf et al., 1992), just before osk/Staufen starts accumulating at the posterior pole.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The anterior-posterior gradient of cortical microtubule results in slightly more microtubule plus ends oriented towards the posterior pole.
source: The anterior-posterior gradient of cortical microtubule results in slightly more microtubule plus ends oriented towards the posterior pole (Nashchekin et al., 2016; Zimyanin et al., 2008; Parton et al., 2011; Khuc Trong et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-1 has been proposed to drive osk mRNA transport along weakly biased cortical microtubules, favoring osk mRNA movement from the anterior to the posterior pole.
source: Kinesin-1 has been proposed to drive osk mRNA transport along these weakly biased cortical microtubules, favoring osk mRNA movement from the anterior to the posterior pole (Brendza et al., 2000; Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Zimyanin et al., 2008; Khuc Trong et al., 2015; Nieuwburg et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-1 has another essential function in reorganizing microtubules.
source: In addition to its conventional cargo-transporting activity, kinesin-1 has another essential function in reorganizing microtubules.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Kinesin-1 slides antiparallel microtubules against each other in many cell types using its N-terminal motor domain and a second microtubule-binding site at the C-terminus of kinesin-1 heavy chain (KHC).
source: Using its N-terminal motor domain and a second microtubule-binding site at the C-terminus of kinesin-1 heavy chain (KHC), kinesin-1 slides antiparallel microtubules against each other in many cell types (Jolly et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2015; Winding et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-driven microtubule sliding together with kinesin-driven cargo transport generates the force that drives fast cytoplasmic streaming of the ooplasm in late-stage Drosophila oocytes.
source: Kinesin-driven microtubule sliding together with kinesin-driven cargo transport generates the force that drives fast cytoplasmic streaming of the ooplasm in late-stage Drosophila oocytes (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Diffusion facilitated by streaming, rather than directed transport along microtubules, is responsible for the localization of posterior determinants during late oogenesis.
source: Diffusion facilitated by streaming, rather than directed transport along microtubules, is responsible for the localization of posterior determinants during late oogenesis (Lu et al., 2018; Glotzer et al., 1997; Forrest and Gavis, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Directed transport and streaming are not sufficient for stable osk/Staufen accumulation at the posterior pole; an anchorage mechanism is required.
source: Despite the necessity of directed transport and streaming, they are not sufficient for stable osk/Staufen accumulation at the posterior pole; an anchorage mechanism is required to counteract both diffusion and shear forces of the streaming ooplasm that can displace osk/Staufen from the posterior cap.
evidence: This statement is supported by logical inference from the experimental context.

claim: osk mRNA anchorage has been suggested to be actin-dependent.
source: osk mRNA anchorage has been suggested to be actin-dependent.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cortical localization of osk/Staufen is significantly reduced upon F-actin fragmentation.
source: Cortical localization of osk/Staufen is significantly reduced upon F-actin fragmentation (Cha et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V (didum in Drosophila) is involved in osk mRNA cortical localization.
source: An actin motor, myosin-V (didum in Drosophila), is involved in osk mRNA cortical localization (Krauss et al., 2009; Sinsimer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V is uniformly localized at the oocyte cortex.
source: However, myosin-V is uniformly localized at the oocyte cortex (Krauss et al., 2009); it is not clear why a uniformly distributed cortical anchor attaches osk/Staufen only at the posterior pole.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Genetic data suggest that kinesin-1 activity antagonizes the function of myosin-V as a cortical anchor.
source: Genetic data suggest that kinesin-1 activity antagonizes the function of myosin-V as a cortical anchor (Krauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Competition between long-distance transport along microtubules by kinesins and anchorage/local transport by myosin-V can direct the distribution of cellular cargoes in several biological systems including neurons and pigment cells (melanophores).
source: In several other biological systems including neurons and pigment cells (melanophores), competition between long-distance transport along microtubules by kinesins and anchorage/local transport by myosin-V can direct the distribution of cellular cargoes (Rogers and Gelfand, 1998; Wu et al., 1998; Kapitein et al., 2013; van Bergeijk et al., 2015; Pathak et al., 2010; Bridgman, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-1 has been proposed to actively remove osk mRNA from the cortex (cortical exclusion) by transporting it along cortical-anchored microtubules towards plus-ends of microtubules in the cytoplasm.
source: In the oocyte, kinesin-1 has been proposed to actively remove osk mRNA from the cortex (cortical exclusion) by transporting it along cortical-anchored microtubules towards plus-ends of microtubules in the cytoplasm (Cha et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of KHC by RNAi leads to uniform cortical localization of Staufen in the oocyte.
source: Knockdown of KHC by RNAi leads to uniform cortical localization of Staufen in the oocyte (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1D; Brendza et al., 2000; Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Lu et al., 2018; Cha et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1D and citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-1 activity is essential for Staufen cortical exclusion from the anterior and lateral cortex.
source: This indicates that kinesin-1 activity is essential for Staufen cortical exclusion from the anterior and lateral cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi knockdown data.

claim: KhcΔHinge2 is a constitutively active KHC mutant that lacks the flexible hinge region (residues 521–642) and is unable to fold into an auto-inhibited conformation.
source: To increase kinesin-1 activity in the oocyte, we employed a previously characterized constitutively active KHC mutant, KhcΔHinge2, which lacks the flexible hinge region (residues 521–642). As a result, it is unable to fold into an auto-inhibited conformation, resulting in constitutive activation (Figure 1A; Barlan et al., 2013; Kelliher et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Heterozygotes carrying one copy of KhcΔHinge2 exhibit a more loosened posterior Staufen cap in stage 9 oocytes.
source: Staufen staining of heterozygotes carrying one copy of KhcΔHinge2 exhibits a more loosened posterior Staufen cap in stage 9 oocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, G and I)), demonstrating that constitutively active kinesin-1 is dominant, and sufficient to partially mislocalize Staufen from the posterior crescent.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, G and I.

claim: Constitutively active kinesin-1 is dominant and sufficient to partially mislocalize Staufen from the posterior crescent.
source: Staufen staining of heterozygotes carrying one copy of KhcΔHinge2 exhibits a more loosened posterior Staufen cap in stage 9 oocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, G and I)), demonstrating that constitutively active kinesin-1 is dominant, and sufficient to partially mislocalize Staufen from the posterior crescent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the heterozygote data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, G and I.

claim: In KhcΔHinge2 homozygous mutants, Staufen is mislocalized in stage 9 oocytes, typically forming a large aggregate in the middle of the oocyte and a small loose residual cap near the posterior cortex.
source: Within these KhcΔHinge2 homozygous germline clones, Staufen is mislocalized in stage 9 oocytes. Typically, Staufen forms a large aggregate in the middle of the oocyte and a small loose residual cap near the posterior cortex (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1B–E.

claim: At stage 10B, normal Staufen distribution is recovered in KhcΔHinge2 homozygous mutants with the restoration of the posterior cap and clearing of the central cytoplasmic aggregate.
source: Intriguingly, later in development (at stage 10B) normal Staufen distribution is recovered with the restoration of the posterior cap and clearing of the central cytoplasmic aggregate (Figure 1F–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, H and J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1F–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, H and J.

claim: Osk protein, translated at the posterior pole, functions in a positive feedback mechanism for osk/Staufen accumulation in streaming oocytes.
source: Previous studies suggest that Osk protein, translated at the posterior pole, functions in a positive feedback mechanism for osk/Staufen accumulation in streaming oocytes (Lu et al., 2018; Vanzo and Ephrussi, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: osk/Staufen posterior localization is sensitive to kinesin-1 activity level.
source: Together, our data show that osk/Staufen posterior localization is sensitive to kinesin-1 activity level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on kinesin-1 manipulation.

claim: Inhibition of myosin-V by overexpression of the C-terminal myosin-V globular tail (GT) causes Staufen mislocalization to the center of the oocyte.
source: Previous studies reveal that inhibition of myosin-V by overexpression of the C-terminal myosin-V globular tail (GT) causes Staufen mislocalization to the center of the oocyte (Krauss et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2018), which is in agreement with our hypothesis that myosin-V anchors osk/Staufen at the posterior cortex.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V is auto-inhibited through its C-terminal cargo-binding GT domain binding to the motor and inhibiting its motor ATPase activity.
source: Similar to kinesin-1, myosin-V is auto-inhibited through its C-terminal cargo-binding GT domain binding to the motor and inhibiting its motor ATPase activity (Thirumurugan et al., 2006; Donovan and Bretscher, 2015; Li et al., 2008; Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The C-terminus of the coiled-coil 1 region is essential for auto-inhibition of myosin-V as it docks the cargo-binding tail for binding to the motor domain, stabilizing the closed inactive conformation.
source: The C-terminus of the coiled-coil 1 region is essential for auto-inhibition as it docks the cargo-binding tail for binding to the motor domain, stabilizing the closed inactive conformation (Figure 2A; Donovan and Bretscher, 2015; Li et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminus of the coiled-coil 1 region of mouse myosin Va abolishes the inhibitory function of the GT domain and leads to constitutive activity of myosin-Va.
source: Deletion of the C-terminus of the coiled-coil 1 region of mouse myosin Va abolishes the inhibitory function of the GT domain and leads to constitutive activity of myosin-Va (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MyoVΔ1017-1114 shows a similar velocity in actin gliding assays compared to wild-type full-length myosin-V.
source: MyoVΔ1017-1114 shows a similar velocity in actin gliding assays compared to wild-type full-length myosin-V (Figure 2B), indicating that the deletion does not disrupt myosin-V motor function.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The deletion in MyoVΔ1017-1114 does not disrupt myosin-V motor function.
source: MyoVΔ1017-1114 shows a similar velocity in actin gliding assays compared to wild-type full-length myosin-V (Figure 2B), indicating that the deletion does not disrupt myosin-V motor function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the actin gliding assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type myosin-V displays a low ATPase activity in the absence of Ca2+ as it adopts a closed inactive conformation.
source: Wild-type myosin-V displays a low ATPase activity in the absence of Ca2+, as it adopts a closed inactive conformation (Li et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2004), but it is significantly stimulated by Ca2+ due to release from the auto-inhibited conformation (Wang et al., 2004; Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wild-type myosin-V ATPase activity is significantly stimulated by Ca2+ due to release from the auto-inhibited conformation.
source: Wild-type myosin-V displays a low ATPase activity in the absence of Ca2+, as it adopts a closed inactive conformation (Li et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2004), but it is significantly stimulated by Ca2+ due to release from the auto-inhibited conformation (Wang et al., 2004; Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MyoVΔ1017-1114 displays an equivalent and high level of ATPase activity with and without Ca2+, suggesting the deletion mutant is constitutively active.
source: In contrast, MyoVΔ1017-1114 displays an equivalent and high level of ATPase activity with and without Ca2+, suggesting the deletion mutant is constitutively active (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most wild-type myosin-V molecules at a low salt concentration adopt a closed conformation.
source: Most wild-type myosin-V molecules at a low salt concentration adopt a closed conformation (Figure 2E and I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while in high salt concentration they display an open conformation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This statement is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2E, I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Wild-type myosin-V displays an open conformation in high salt concentration.
source: Most wild-type myosin-V molecules at a low salt concentration adopt a closed conformation (Figure 2E and I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while in high salt concentration they display an open conformation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This statement is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The closed conformation of wild-type myosin-V observed in low salt closely resembles that previously demonstrated in mammalian myosin Va, indicating that the structural basis for autoinhibition is conserved.
source: The closed conformation of wild-type myosin-V observed in low salt closely resembles that previously demonstrated in mammalian myosin Va, indicating that the structural basis for autoinhibition is conserved (Thirumurugan et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electron microscopy data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Myosin-VΔ1017-1114 displays an open conformation in both low and high salt conditions.
source: In contrast, myosin-VΔ1017-1114 displays an open conformation in both low and high salt conditions (Figure 2G–H and J).
evidence: This statement is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G–H and J.

claim: The Δ1017–1114 deletion results in a more open conformation than wild-type myosin-V.
source: Measurement of head-junction-head angles shows that the Δ1017–1114 deletion results in a more open conformation than wild-type myosin-V (Figure 2K) (see more details in Materials and methods 'Electron Microscopy').
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The Δ1017–1114 deletion creates a constitutively active myosin-V.
source: Collectively, the data show that the Δ1017–1114 deletion creates a constitutively active myosin-V.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including ATPase assays and electron microscopy.

claim: Expressing MyoVΔ1017-1114 in didum[88] germline clones causes Staufen staining to become less restricted at the posterior pole and spread to the lateral cortex.
source: We expressed MyoVΔ1017-1114 in didum[88] germline clones and find that Staufen staining in these oocytes becomes less restricted at the posterior pole and spreads to the lateral cortex (Figure 2L–N).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2L–N.

claim: The effect of constitutively active myosin-V on Staufen localization is more pronounced at the anterior half of the lateral cortex.
source: The effect is more pronounced at the anterior half of the lateral cortex (Figure 2M–N).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2M–N.

claim: Constitutively active myosin-V expands the domain of cortically anchored osk/Staufen beyond the posterior pole.
source: Thus, in agreement with the proposed role of myosin-V as an anchor for osk/Staufen at the actin cortex, constitutively active myosin-V expands the domain of cortically anchored osk/Staufen beyond the posterior pole.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the constitutively active myosin-V data.

claim: osk/Staufen cortical anchorage is sensitive to myosin-V activity level.
source: Together, these results indicate that osk/Staufen cortical anchorage is sensitive to myosin-V activity level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on myosin-V manipulation.

claim: The proper balance of kinesin-1 and myosin-V activities is essential for osk/Staufen localization at the posterior pole.
source: The results above demonstrate that the proper balance of kinesin-1 and myosin-V activities is essential for osk/Staufen localization at the posterior pole, consistent with the competition model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on both kinesin-1 and myosin-V manipulation.

claim: Neither actin filaments nor myosin-V are concentrated at the posterior pole in the oocyte.
source: In the oocyte, neither actin filaments nor myosin-V are concentrated at the posterior pole (Krauss et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–1F.

claim: The microtubule network in the oocyte displays a clear anterior-posterior gradient, with the lowest density of cortical microtubules at the posterior cortex.
source: In contrast, the microtubule network in the oocyte displays a clear anterior-posterior gradient, with the lowest density of cortical microtubules at the posterior cortex (Clark et al., 1997; Nashchekin et al., 2016; Zimyanin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The anterior-posterior microtubule gradient is revealed by microtubule labeling with germline-specific expressed EMTB-3XTagRFP.
source: This anterior-posterior (A-P) microtubule gradient is revealed by microtubule labeling with germline-specific expressed EMTB-3XTagRFP (Faire et al., 1999; Figure 3A), and a GFP-labeled endogenous MAP, Jupiter-GFP (Morin et al., 2001; Karpova et al., 2006; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The anterior-posterior microtubule gradient is revealed by a GFP-labeled endogenous MAP, Jupiter-GFP.
source: This anterior-posterior (A-P) microtubule gradient is revealed by microtubule labeling with germline-specific expressed EMTB-3XTagRFP (Faire et al., 1999; Figure 3A), and a GFP-labeled endogenous MAP, Jupiter-GFP (Morin et al., 2001; Karpova et al., 2006; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The microtubule gradient is a result of reduced accumulation of the microtubule minus-end binding protein, Patronin, at the posterior pole.
source: This gradient is a result of reduced accumulation of the microtubule minus-end binding protein, Patronin, at the posterior pole (Figure 3B–C; Nashchekin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B–C and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Germline overexpression of Klp10A leads to complete depolymerization of microtubules in the oocyte as well in the nurse cells, while the somatic follicle cells in these ovaries still have intact microtubules.
source: Germline overexpression of a depolymerizing kinesin, kinesin 13 (Klp10A in Drosophila) (Goshima and Vale, 2005; Mennella et al., 2005), leads to complete depolymerization of microtubules in the oocyte as well in the nurse cells, while the somatic follicle cells in these ovaries still have intact microtubules (Figure 3E–E', compared to Figure 3D–D'; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C' and E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3E–E', Figure 3D–D', and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C' and E.

claim: Lack of microtubules in the oocyte results in a failure of Staufen enrichment at the posterior pole; instead it is uniformly localized along the entire oocyte cortex.
source: This lack of microtubules in the oocyte results in a failure of Staufen enrichment at the posterior pole; instead it is uniformly localized along the entire oocyte cortex (Figure 3G–H and J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3G–H and J.

claim: Patronin stabilizes microtubules and prevents minus-end depolymerization by Klp10A.
source: Patronin stabilizes microtubules and prevents minus-end depolymerization by Klp10A (Goodwin and Vale, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpressing Patronin significantly increases microtubule density in the oocyte.
source: Overexpressing Patronin significantly increases microtubule density in the oocyte (Figure 3F–F'; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3F–F' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–1E.

claim: Increased microtubule density caused by Patronin overexpression causes Staufen to be excluded from the entire cortex and form aggregates in the center of the oocyte where most microtubules plus-ends are directed.
source: This increase in microtubule density causes Staufen to be excluded from the entire cortex. Instead, it forms aggregates in the center of the oocyte where most microtubules plus-ends are directed (Figure 3G, I and K).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3G, I and K.

claim: osk/Staufen localization is controlled by the microtubule density in the oocyte.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that osk/Staufen localization is controlled by the microtubule density in the oocyte.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on microtubule density manipulation.

claim: Decreased density of cortical microtubules favors myosin-V resulting in uniform cortical localization of osk/Staufen.
source: Decreased density of cortical microtubules favors myosin-V resulting in uniform cortical localization of osk/Staufen, whereas increased microtubule density favors kinesin-1 resulting in exclusion of osk/Staufen from the cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on microtubule density manipulation.

claim: Increased microtubule density favors kinesin-1 resulting in exclusion of osk/Staufen from the cortex.
source: Decreased density of cortical microtubules favors myosin-V resulting in uniform cortical localization of osk/Staufen, whereas increased microtubule density favors kinesin-1 resulting in exclusion of osk/Staufen from the cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on microtubule density manipulation.

claim: Locally recruiting Klp10A to the lateral cortex significantly decreases the EMTB-3XTagRFP signal.
source: We combined the microtubule labeling EMTB-3XTagRFP with Klp10A local recruitment, and found that locally recruiting Klp10A to the lateral cortex significantly decreases the EMTB-3XTagRFP signal (Figure 4 —Videos 2 and 3; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—Videos 2 and 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recruitment of Klp10A-SspB to the lateral cortex leads to a dramatic accumulation of RFP-Staufen in the stimulated area.
source: Recruitment of Klp10A-SspB to the lateral cortex leads to a dramatic accumulation of RFP-Staufen in the stimulated area (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: RFP-Staufen progressively accumulated at the cortex over the time of Klp10A stimulation.
source: Over the time of stimulation, the RFP-Staufen progressively accumulated at the cortex (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: The ectopic recruitment of Staufen to the region of reduced microtubule density is reversible.
source: Remarkably, this ectopic recruitment of Staufen to the region of reduced microtubule density is reversible; the Staufen signal decreased to control levels after removal of blue light.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: The ectopic recruitment of Staufen to the region of reduced microtubule density is repeatable.
source: Furthermore, this ectopic recruitment is repeatable. We are able to induce the recruitment either at a single spot of an oocyte (Figure 4 — Videos 4 and 5) or at different spots (Figure 4 —Video 6).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—Videos 4, 5, and 6.

claim: In samples expressing LifeAct-SsrA only (No Klp10A-SspB), no increase of RFP-Staufen is observed after the identical light treatment.
source: In contrast, in the samples expressing LifeAct-SsrA only (No Klp10A-SspB), no increase of RFP-Staufen is observed after the identical light treatment, indicating the effect of Staufen-accumulation is specific to Klp10A recruitment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by control data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The effect of Staufen-accumulation is specific to Klp10A recruitment.
source: In contrast, in the samples expressing LifeAct-SsrA only (No Klp10A-SspB), no increase of RFP-Staufen is observed after the identical light treatment, indicating the effect of Staufen-accumulation is specific to Klp10A recruitment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control experiment data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: After colcemid treatment, no visible microtubules remain at the cortex.
source: After colcemid treatment, no visible microtubules remain at the cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under colcemid treatment conditions, Klp10A recruitment at the actin cortex does not cause Staufen recruitment.
source: Under these conditions, Klp10A recruitment at the actin cortex does not cause Staufen recruitment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Local microtubule density is the key determinant of osk/Staufen localization by tipping the balance of kinesin-myosin competition.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that local microtubule density is the key determinant of osk/Staufen localization by tipping the balance of kinesin-myosin competition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Lower microtubule density favors cortical anchorage by myosin-V.
source: Lower microtubule density favors cortical anchorage by myosin-V, while higher microtubule density favors cortical exclusion by kinesin-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Higher microtubule density favors cortical exclusion by kinesin-1.
source: Lower microtubule density favors cortical anchorage by myosin-V, while higher microtubule density favors cortical exclusion by kinesin-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Upon addition of rapalog, the distribution of KHC576 changes dramatically; it mostly accumulates at the posterior pole, resembling the localization of osk/Staufen.
source: Upon addition of rapalog, the distribution of KHC576 changes dramatically; it mostly accumulates at the posterior pole, resembling the localization of osk/Staufen (Figure 5B and D–D').
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and D–D'.

claim: In the absence of microtubules, the dimerized KHC576-MyoVHMM shows no accumulation at the posterior pole.
source: As a control, we repeated the rapalog treatment after microtubule depolymerization by colcemid. In the absence of microtubules, the dimerized KHC576-MyoVHMM shows no accumulation at the posterior pole (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by control data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A synthetic protein complex containing just two active motors, kinesin-1 and myosin-V, exhibits microtubule-dependent posterior localization in Drosophila oocytes.
source: In summary, our rapalog experiments reveal that a synthetic protein complex containing just two active motors, kinesin-1 and myosin-V, exhibits microtubule-dependent posterior localization in Drosophila oocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rapalog dimerization experiments.

claim: The dimerized KHC576-MyoVHMM complex is removed by kinesin-1 from the anterior-lateral cortex that has more cortical microtubules and trapped by myosin-V at the posterior cortex where the cortical microtubule density is much lower.
source: This dimerized complex is removed by kinesin-1 from the anterior-lateral cortex that has more cortical microtubules and trapped by myosin-V at the posterior cortex where the cortical microtubule density is much lower (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rapalog dimerization experiments and illustrated in Figure 5E.

claim: Direct competition between two motors, kinesin-1 and myosin-V, ensures the posterior anchorage of osk/Staufen.
source: In this study, we combined genetic and optogenetic tools to demonstrate that direct competition between two motors, kinesin-1 and myosin-V, ensures the posterior anchorage of osk/Staufen.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The outcome of the kinesin-myosin competition is primarily determined by the density of cortical microtubules.
source: Notably, we demonstrate that the outcome of the competition is primarily determined by the density of cortical microtubules.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: High microtubule density at the anterior and lateral cortex favors kinesin-driven osk/Staufen cortical exclusion.
source: High microtubule density at the anterior and lateral cortex favors kinesin-driven osk/Staufen cortical exclusion, while low microtubule density at the posterior pole favors myosin-driven cortical retention.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Low microtubule density at the posterior pole favors myosin-driven cortical retention.
source: High microtubule density at the anterior and lateral cortex favors kinesin-driven osk/Staufen cortical exclusion, while low microtubule density at the posterior pole favors myosin-driven cortical retention.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The kinesin-myosin competition and cortical microtubule density together determine the initial accumulation of osk mRNA at the posterior pole.
source: Therefore, the kinesin-myosin competition and cortical microtubule density together determine the initial accumulation of osk mRNA at the posterior pole (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence and illustrated in Figure 5E.

claim: The cortical exclusion model was first proposed after uniform cortical localization of osk mRNA was observed in the kinesin-null oocytes.
source: The cortical exclusion model was first proposed after uniform cortical localization of osk mRNA was observed in the kinesin-null oocytes (Cha et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Constitutively active kinesin-1 causes osk/Staufen mislocalization in the cytoplasm of the oocyte.
source: In agreement with this model, we show that constitutively active kinesin-1 causes osk/Staufen mislocalization in the cytoplasm of the oocyte (Figure 1), whereas reducing microtubule density at the lateral cortex leads to ectopic accumulation of Staufen at the cortex (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reducing microtubule density at the lateral cortex leads to ectopic accumulation of Staufen at the cortex.
source: In agreement with this model, we show that constitutively active kinesin-1 causes osk/Staufen mislocalization in the cytoplasm of the oocyte (Figure 1), whereas reducing microtubule density at the lateral cortex leads to ectopic accumulation of Staufen at the cortex (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Kinesin-1 has been proposed to transport osk/Staufen particles along slightly biased cortical microtubules, resulting in net movement of osk/Staufen from the anterior side to the posterior pole in stage 8–9 oocytes.
source: Previously, several groups have proposed that kinesin-1 transports osk/Staufen particles along slightly biased cortical microtubules, resulting in net movement of osk/Staufen from the anterior side to the posterior pole in stage 8–9 oocytes (Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Lu et al., 2018; Zimyanin et al., 2008; Parton et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-driven cortical exclusion and kinesin-driven transport towards the posterior pole are not mutually exclusive; they describe the same event of osk/Staufen movement.
source: In fact, kinesin-driven cortical exclusion and kinesin-driven transport towards the posterior pole are not mutually exclusive; they describe the same event of osk/Staufen movement.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the understanding of the mechanism.

claim: Within the oocyte, cortical microtubules are anchored to the cortex by their minus-ends while their plus-ends face towards the cytoplasm.
source: Within the oocyte, cortical microtubules are anchored to the cortex by their minus-ends while their plus-ends face towards the cytoplasm.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Kinesin-1-driven transport along microtubules is a prerequisite for kinesin-1-driven cortical exclusion.
source: Thus, kinesin-1-driven transport along microtubules is a prerequisite for kinesin-1-driven cortical exclusion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the understanding of the mechanism.

claim: Cortical exclusion of osk/Staufen by kinesin-1 results in biased transport of osk/Staufen towards the posterior pole.
source: Cortical exclusion of osk/Staufen by kinesin-1 results in biased transport of osk/Staufen towards the posterior pole (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the understanding of the mechanism and illustrated in Figure 5E.

claim: Increasing KHC dosage enhances osk/Staufen mislocalization phenotypes in myosin-V loss-of-function mutants.
source: This kinesin-myosin competition model is suggested by genetic interaction data from a previous study. Specifically, increasing KHC dosage enhances osk/Staufen mislocalization phenotypes in myosin-V loss-of-function mutants, while reducing KHC dosage by half partially suppresses myosin loss-of-function phenotypes (Krauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Reducing KHC dosage by half partially suppresses myosin loss-of-function phenotypes.
source: This kinesin-myosin competition model is suggested by genetic interaction data from a previous study. Specifically, increasing KHC dosage enhances osk/Staufen mislocalization phenotypes in myosin-V loss-of-function mutants, while reducing KHC dosage by half partially suppresses myosin loss-of-function phenotypes (Krauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Double MyoV and Khc mutant clones have diffuse cytoplasmic localization of osk mRNA, compared to uniform cortical localization of osk mRNA in Khc single mutant clones.
source: Furthermore, double MyoV and Khc mutant clones have diffuse cytoplasmic localization of osk mRNA, compared to uniform cortical localization of osk mRNA in Khc single mutant clones (Krauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of kinesin-1, myosin-V promiscuously anchors osk/Staufen everywhere in the cortex.
source: These data strongly imply that in the absence of kinesin-1, myosin-V promiscuously anchors osk/Staufen everywhere in the cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data cited from previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for melanosomes.
source: For instance, myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for melanosomes (Rogers and Gelfand, 1998; Wu et al., 1998; Wu et al., 1997), peroxisomes (Kapitein et al., 2013; van Bergeijk et al., 2015), recycling endosomes (van Bergeijk et al., 2015), mitochondria (Pathak et al., 2010), and synaptic vesicles (Bridgman, 1999) at sites of local accumulation of F-actin.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for peroxisomes.
source: For instance, myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for melanosomes (Rogers and Gelfand, 1998; Wu et al., 1998; Wu et al., 1997), peroxisomes (Kapitein et al., 2013; van Bergeijk et al., 2015), recycling endosomes (van Bergeijk et al., 2015), mitochondria (Pathak et al., 2010), and synaptic vesicles (Bridgman, 1999) at sites of local accumulation of F-actin.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for recycling endosomes.
source: For instance, myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for melanosomes (Rogers and Gelfand, 1998; Wu et al., 1998; Wu et al., 1997), peroxisomes (Kapitein et al., 2013; van Bergeijk et al., 2015), recycling endosomes (van Bergeijk et al., 2015), mitochondria (Pathak et al., 2010), and synaptic vesicles (Bridgman, 1999) at sites of local accumulation of F-actin.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for mitochondria.
source: For instance, myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for melanosomes (Rogers and Gelfand, 1998; Wu et al., 1998; Wu et al., 1997), peroxisomes (Kapitein et al., 2013; van Bergeijk et al., 2015), recycling endosomes (van Bergeijk et al., 2015), mitochondria (Pathak et al., 2010), and synaptic vesicles (Bridgman, 1999) at sites of local accumulation of F-actin.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for synaptic vesicles.
source: For instance, myosin-V opposes microtubule-dependent transport and provides a dynamic anchor for melanosomes (Rogers and Gelfand, 1998; Wu et al., 1998; Wu et al., 1997), peroxisomes (Kapitein et al., 2013; van Bergeijk et al., 2015), recycling endosomes (van Bergeijk et al., 2015), mitochondria (Pathak et al., 2010), and synaptic vesicles (Bridgman, 1999) at sites of local accumulation of F-actin.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At sites of local accumulation of F-actin, the abundance of F-actin tracks provides an upper hand for myosin-V to win the tug-of-wars over microtubule motors.
source: At these sites, the abundance of F-actin tracks provides an upper hand for myosin-V to win the tug-of-wars over microtubule motors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the understanding of kinesin-myosin competition in other systems.

claim: Kinesin-myosin competition appears to be an evolutionarily conserved mechanism to allow flexible refinement and/or error correction, as motors constantly undergo reversible binding and releasing activity on cytoskeletal filaments.
source: Kinesin-myosin competition appears to be an evolutionarily conserved mechanism to allow flexible refinement and/or error correction, as motors constantly undergo reversible binding and releasing activity on cytoskeletal filaments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary significance of the mechanism.

claim: F-actin density is uniform along the oocyte cortex.
source: In the oocytes, the machinery responsible for osk/Staufen localization contains the same basic building blocks; however, unlike the other systems, the outcome of the competition is not determined by actin filament density, as F-actin density is uniform along the oocyte cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Synthetic motor domains of a plus-end motor, kinesin-1, and a minus-end motor, kinesin-14/Nod, were used to label overall microtubule polarity in Drosophila oocytes and neurons.
source: Previously, synthetic motor domains of a plus-end motor, kinesin-1, and a minus-end motor, kinesin-14/Nod, were used to label overall microtubule polarity in Drosophila oocytes and neurons (Kin:βGal and Nod:βGal) (Clark et al., 1994; Clark et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Direct competition (without any cargo binding) between a microtubule motor, kinesin-1, and an actin motor, myosin-V, is sufficient for initial posterior localization in a Drosophila oocyte.
source: Together, using dimerized synthetic motors, we demonstrate that direct competition (without any cargo binding) between a microtubule motor, kinesin-1, and an actin motor, myosin-V, is sufficient for initial posterior localization in a Drosophila oocyte.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by the rapalog dimerization experiments.

claim: Two cytoskeletal components (microtubules and F-actin) and two molecular motors (kinesin-1 and myosin-V) govern the posterior determination for future Drosophila embryos.
source: Together, two cytoskeletal components (microtubules and F-actin) and two molecular motors (kinesin-1 and myosin-V) govern the posterior determination for future Drosophila embryos.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, summarizing the key findings.
